text: He says the kidneys filter the blood many times each day, citing an estimate of about 37 to 40 times.
Using an adult blood volume of about five liters, he estimates that the kidneys process roughly 180 to 200 liters of fluid per day.
From that, he argues that drinking many extra liters of water does not meaningfully 'clean' or stimulate the kidneys.
He rejects the idea that the kidneys are 'washed' by water, sugarcane juice, malt drinks, or barley beverages.
He says these popular claims are not scientifically supported, and he also disputes the idea that drinking more water directly moisturizes the skin or hair.
He explains that the outer skin is made largely of dead, dry cells and acts as a barrier that helps reduce water loss from the body.
He says that when skin feels dry, topical products such as oils or wax-like moisturizers are used rather than simply adding more drinking water.
He argues that the moisturizing effect of such products comes mainly from fats and waxes, not from water itself.
He cautions against repeating health advice without questioning its evidence, including the idea that drinking very large amounts of water is always healthier.
He questions why the body would need excessive water intake if thirst already provides a natural signal for when to drink.
He says the body regulates water needs partly through blood concentration and thirst, and he recommends drinking in response to thirst rather than forcing large quantities.
He adds that the body also produces a small amount of metabolic water as a by-product of normal metabolism.
He points out that urination continues even during fasting, which he uses to illustrate that the body still generates and handles water internally.

He concludes that, in his view, the body generally regulates water well and does not necessarily need more than what thirst signals. This is his interpretation and should not replace medical advice about hydration or kidney disease.
